faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Laurens attics?

faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Laurens attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Gray Court?

We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: There are bats in my Waterloo attic. When can they be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are excluded, never trapped or killed, and South Carolina requires no permit to remove them. Timing follows SCDNR guidance rather than a state ban: complete exclusions are scheduled for early spring (March–April) or late summer into fall (August–October), because excluding in May through mid-July can trap flightless pups inside. In Waterloo we fit one-way exits over the entry points used by colonies near Reedy River and lake-country farms in the county's southwest, seal every other gap of 3/8 inch or more, and clean guano once the colony is out. A single bat found in living quarters is different — do not handle it, and it should go to the SC Department of Public Health for rabies testing.

faqs.q: An armadillo is burrowing under my Waterloo porch. What do you do?
faqs.a: Armadillos dig to sleep and to escape heat, and the shaded soil under a Waterloo porch near Reedy River and lake-country farms in the county's southwest is prime burrow ground. We trap the resident animal — armadillos are handled under depredation rules, since routine relocation is against state law — and then screen the burrow line so a replacement cannot dig back in along the same run.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Waterloo actually involve?
